claims.statement: In the NSABP P-1 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled prevention trial in women at increased breast cancer risk, tamoxifen 20 mg/day reduced the cumulative incidence of invasive breast cancer by 49% (43.4 per 1,000 women on placebo vs. 22.0 per 1,000 on tamoxifen through 69 months) and reduced estrogen-receptor-positive tumor incidence by 69%, but this benefit came with an increased rate of endometrial cancer (risk ratio 2.53) and elevated rates of stroke, pulmonary embolism, and deep-vein thrombosis, particularly in women aged 50 and older.

context.population: women at increased risk of breast cancer (NSABP P-1 cohort)

claims.statement: In the ATLAS randomized trial of women with ER-positive breast cancer already on adjuvant tamoxifen, continuing tamoxifen to 10 years versus stopping at 5 years further reduced breast cancer recurrence (18.0% vs 20.8%; RR 0.84) and breast cancer mortality (18.6% vs 21.1% cumulative; RR 0.87), but roughly doubled the cumulative incidence of endometrial cancer (1.80% vs 0.97%; RR 1.74).

context.population: women with ER-positive breast cancer already completing 5 years of adjuvant tamoxifen
context.useCase: extended adjuvant duration (10 vs 5 years) after breast cancer diagnosis

claims.statement: Tamoxifen (Nolvadex) is widely marketed and self-administered in bodybuilding/anabolic-androgenic-steroid (AAS) communities as unsupervised 'post-cycle therapy' (PCT) to restore endogenous testosterone and manage gynecomastia after steroid cycles, despite no evidence-based clinical guidelines supporting this specific use; a 2025 qualitative analysis of illegal and falsified PCT medicines found frequent adverse events among AAS users self-administering SERMs, and product-testing of illicit tamoxifen samples found some were incorrectly labeled or substituted with non-active ingredients, indicating both an efficacy/safety evidence gap and a product-integrity risk distinct from the FDA-approved, prescription, pharmacy-dispensed product.

context.population: anabolic-androgenic steroid users self-administering unsupervised PCT
context.formulation: illicitly sourced tamoxifen, often unverified purity/labeling
context.useCase: bodybuilding post-cycle testosterone recovery / gynecomastia management (not an FDA-approved indication)

extractedEvidence.quote: since no evidence-based recommendations for safe AAS withdrawal management currently exist, some users self-administer non-approved post-cycle therapy (PCT) to stimulate endogenous testicular function.

The main adverse events reported by male AAS users to SERMs (clomiphene and tamoxifen) were decreased libido and erectile dysfunction (24%), acne (21%), fatigue (19%), mood disorders (13%), visual disturbances (5%), arthralgia (4%), insomnia (4%), and hot flushes (2%).
Among the 63 samples, seven with declared tamoxifen were tested; five contained the declared API, while two were incorrectly labeled.
the self-administration of unapproved PCT using illegal and falsified medicines is dangerous and can be considered a potential threat to consumer health

reviewFlags: misinformation-adjacent: popular PCT/gynecomastia marketing claims lack a controlled human evidence base establishing efficacy for this specific unsupervised use pattern
distinguish clearly from the FDA-approved, prescription-dispensed indications documented elsewhere in this packet
quotes extracted via automated page summarization; verify exact wording against the Frontiers full-text PDF at review time

conflicts.summary: Extending adjuvant tamoxifen from 5 to 10 years (ATLAS trial) reduces breast cancer recurrence and mortality but nearly doubles endometrial cancer incidence; the ATLAS figures in this packet were extracted from a secondary trial-summary page rather than the primary Lancet full text, so the underlying numbers require confirmation against the original publication before this benefit/risk trade-off is finalized for publication.

Popular online marketing frames tamoxifen (Nolvadex) as a bodybuilding PCT/gynecomastia agent, while the only FDA-approved, evidence-backed uses are breast cancer treatment, DCIS, and risk reduction in high-risk women; no controlled human trial evidence in this packet establishes efficacy or safety for unsupervised post-cycle testosterone recovery.
